title: Magnetic Anisotropy and Magnetization Dynamics in Si/Ni Multilayers Probed by FMR and VSM Magnetometry
authors: Dushyant Singh, Subha Maity, Tharundev V, Subhavenkadesh SS, Vigneshwari SR, Krista R. Khiangte
abstract: The magnetic anisotropy and magnetization dynamics of sputtered [Si(40~Å)/Ni($t_{\mathrm{Ni}}$~Å)]$_{20}$ multilayers were systematically investigated at room temperature using SQUID--VSM magnetometry and angle-dependent ferromagnetic resonance (FMR). Static measurements reveal soft ferromagnetic behaviour in thicker Ni layers and mixed ferromagnetic and superparamagnetic contributions at reduced thicknesses. The saturation magnetization increases toward the bulk Ni value with increasing thickness, consistent with Ni nanocrystallite growth. Magnetic dead-layer analysis yields an interfacial dead-layer thickness of approximately $9$~Å per interface, accounting for the suppressed magnetization in thinner Ni layers. Angle-dependent FMR measurements reveal effective easy-plane magnetic anisotropy, while out-of-plane spectra exhibit additional non-uniform spin-wave modes. The effective magnetization remains lower than the static saturation magnetization, indicating a perpendicular anisotropy contribution that partially compensates the demagnetizing field. Quantitative anisotropy analysis yields an interfacial anisotropy constant of $K_S = +0.17~\mathrm{erg\,cm^{-2}}$, favouring perpendicular magnetization, and a volume anisotropy constant of $K_V = -1.23 \times 10^6~\mathrm{erg\,cm^{-3}}$, favouring in-plane alignment, with an extrapolated anisotropy crossover thickness of $t_c \approx 27$~Å. Increasing FMR line-shape asymmetry with decreasing Ni thickness is consistent with enhanced interfacial roughness. These findings highlight the competing interfacial and volume anisotropies and the importance of Ni thickness and interface quality in tailoring Si/Ni multilayers for silicon-compatible spintronic applications.
summary: This paper experimentally investigates the magnetic anisotropy and magnetization dynamics in Si/Ni multilayers using VSM and FMR. By analyzing thickness dependence, the authors quantify competing interfacial and volume magnetic anisotropies. The findings are critical for understanding how interface quality and layer thickness can be controlled to tailor these materials for silicon-compatible spintronic applications.
main_problem: The study investigates the magnetic anisotropy and magnetization dynamics in Si/Ni multilayers as a function of Ni layer thickness.
main_result: The analysis reveals competing interfacial and volume anisotropies, quantifying an interfacial anisotropy constant ($K_S$) favoring perpendicular magnetization and a volume anisotropy constant ($K_V$) favoring in-plane alignment.
method: The research combines static magnetization measurements (SQUID-VSM) with dynamic measurements (angle-dependent Ferromagnetic Resonance, FMR) to probe magnetic behavior.
model_or_system: The physical system is sputtered [Si(40 Å)/Ni($t_{\mathrm{Ni}}$ Å)]$_{20}$ multilayers deposited on Si(111) substrates. The analysis models the magnetic response using dead-layer approximations and spin-wave theory derived from FMR data.
key_observables: Saturation magnetization ($M_s$), coercivity ($H_c$), interfacial dead-layer thickness ($\delta$), interfacial anisotropy constant ($K_S$), volume anisotropy constant ($K_V$), and spin-wave modes.
important_parameters: Ni layer thickness ($t_{\mathrm{Ni}}$), interface quality, and the crossover thickness ($t_c \approx 27 	ext{ Å}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the magnetic properties are governed by the interplay between interfacial effects (dead layers, $K_S$) and bulk volume effects ($K_V$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate $M-H$ hysteresis loops for $H_c$ determination, $M_s$ vs. $t_{\mathrm{Ni}}$ trends, and FMR spectra showing angular dependence and different spin-wave modes.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes static measurements (VSM) to determine $M_s$ and dead-layer thickness, followed by dynamic measurements (FMR) to quantify anisotropy constants ($K_S, K_V$) and identify different spin-wave excitation modes.
why_interesting: While primarily condensed matter magnetism, the detailed study of interfacial effects and anisotropy control in thin films is crucial for designing functional spintronic devices, which often interface with quantum components.
